report:
**Conclusion: no.** High-quality randomized evidence shows hydroxychloroquine does **not** reduce the likelihood of death from COVID-19; it may slightly increase it.

The strongest single study was the large UK RECOVERY randomized trial in hospitalized patients. Death within 28 days occurred in 421/1,561 (27.0%) assigned hydroxychloroquine versus 790/3,155 (25.0%) assigned usual care (rate ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.97–1.23). This excludes a meaningful mortality benefit in that setting.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926

The broader evidence agrees. An international collaborative meta-analysis of randomized trials found hydroxychloroquine was associated with **increased mortality**, not reduced mortality. Randomization is especially important here because it balances baseline illness severity and other factors that can distort observational comparisons.  
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z

Why did claims of benefit persist? Some early, non-randomized or observational studies reported lower mortality. Those results can reflect confounding—for example, treated and untreated patients may differ in when they sought care, disease severity, co-treatments, and clinical setting. Later large randomized trials were designed to address those biases and did not confirm benefit.

There is also a harm consideration: the FDA cautioned against use outside hospitals or clinical trials because of potentially serious heart-rhythm effects, and it revoked the emergency authorization after determining the drugs were unlikely to be effective for their authorized COVID-19 uses.  
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-cautions-against-use-hydroxychloroquine-or-chloroquine-covid-19-outside-hospital-setting-or  
https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-revokes-emergency-use-authorization-chloroquine-and
